claim: The VR system allows expression of spatial navigation and neuronal firing patterns characteristic of real open arenas.
source: This system allows expression of the spatial navigation and neuronal firing patterns characteristic of real open arenas (R).
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by behavioral and electrophysiological data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Place and grid cell firing had broader spatial tuning in VR compared to R.
source: Comparing VR to R: place and grid, but not head-direction, cell firing had broader spatial tuning
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by quantitative measurements in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Head-direction cell firing did not have broader spatial tuning in VR compared to R.
source: Comparing VR to R: place and grid, but not head-direction, cell firing had broader spatial tuning
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Place cell firing was more directional in VR than in R.
source: place, but not grid, cell firing was more directional
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by directional information measurements in Figure 3.

claim: Grid cell firing was not more directional in VR than in R.
source: place, but not grid, cell firing was more directional
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by directional information measurements in Figure 4.

claim: Theta frequency increased less with running speed in VR compared to R.
source: theta frequency increased less with running speed
evidence: Stated in abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Increases in firing rates with running speed were similar in VR and R.
source: whereas increases in firing rates with running speed and place and grid cells' theta phase precession were similar
evidence: Stated in abstract and shown in Figure 7C-F.

claim: Theta phase precession in place and grid cells was similar in VR and R.
source: whereas increases in firing rates with running speed and place and grid cells' theta phase precession were similar
evidence: Stated in abstract and demonstrated in Figure 8.

claim: Omni-directional place cell firing in R may require local cues unavailable in VR.
source: These results suggest that the omni-directional place cell firing in R may require local-cues unavailable in VR
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the abstract based on the observed increased directionality of place cells in VR.

claim: The scale of grid and place cell firing patterns reflects translational motion inferred from both virtual and real cues.
source: and that the scale of grid and place cell firing patterns, and theta frequency, reflect translational motion inferred from both virtual (visual and proprioceptive) and real (vestibular translation and extra-maze) cues
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the abstract based on the observed changes in spatial scale.

claim: Theta frequency reflects translational motion inferred from both virtual and real cues.
source: and that the scale of grid and place cell firing patterns, and theta frequency, reflect translational motion inferred from both virtual (visual and proprioceptive) and real (vestibular translation and extra-maze) cues
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the abstract based on the observed changes in theta frequency.

claim: Firing rates appear to reflect visual and proprioceptive cues alone.
source: By contrast, firing rates and theta phase precession appear to reflect visual and proprioceptive cues alone.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the abstract based on the similarity of firing rate modulation in VR and R.

claim: Theta phase precession appears to reflect visual and proprioceptive cues alone.
source: By contrast, firing rates and theta phase precession appear to reflect visual and proprioceptive cues alone.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the abstract based on the similarity of theta phase precession in VR and R.

claim: Virtual reality allows experimental control and environmental manipulations impossible in the real world.
source: Virtual reality (VR) offers a powerful tool for investigating spatial cognition, allowing experimental control and environmental manipulations that are impossible in the real world.
evidence: This is a general statement about VR capabilities supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Uncontrolled real-world cues cannot contribute to determining location within the virtual environment.
source: For example, uncontrolled real-world cues cannot contribute to determining location within the virtual environment
evidence: This is a characteristic of VR systems stated as a known property.

claim: VR allows assessment of relative influences of motoric movement signals and visual environmental signals by decoupling them.
source: while the relative influences of motoric movement signals and visual environmental signals can be assessed by decoupling one from the other (Tcheang et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013)
evidence: This capability is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Head-fixed mice allow use of intracellular recording and two photon microscopy.
source: In addition, the ability to study (virtual) spatial navigation in head-fixed mice allows the use of intracellular recording and two photon microscopy (Dombeck et al., 2010; Harvey et al., 2009; Royer et al., 2012; Domnisoru et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013; Heys et al., 2014; Low et al., 2014; Villette et al., 2015; Danielson et al., 2016; Cohen et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated as an advantage and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Modulation of place cell or grid cell firing along a single dimension can be observed in virtual environments explored by head-fixed mice.
source: The modulation of firing of place cells or grid cells along a single dimension, such as distance travelled along a specific trajectory or path, can be observed as virtual environments are explored by head-fixed mice (Chen et al., 2013; Dombeck et al., 2010; Harvey et al., 2009; Domnisoru et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013; Heys et al., 2014; Low et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Two-dimensional firing patterns of place, grid and head-direction cells in real-world open arenas are not seen in systems where the animal cannot physically rotate through 360°.
source: However, the two-dimensional firing patterns of place, grid and head-direction cells in real-world open arenas are not seen in these systems, in which the animal cannot physically rotate through 360°.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous systems based on established knowledge.

claim: Two-dimensional spatial firing patterns of place, head direction, grid and border cells have been observed in VR systems where rats can physically rotate through 360°.
source: By contrast, the two-dimensional (2-d) spatial firing patterns of place, head direction, grid and border cells have been observed in VR systems in which rats can physically rotate through 360°(Aronov and Tank, 2014; Hölscher et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The frequency of the movement-related theta rhythm is reduced in VR systems where rats can rotate 360°.
source: Minor differences with free exploration remain, for example the frequency of the movement-related theta rhythm is reduced (Aronov and Tank, 2014)
evidence: This is stated as a known difference supported by citation.

claim: Reduced theta frequency in VR may be due to the absence of translational vestibular acceleration signals.
source: perhaps due to the absence of translational vestibular acceleration signals (Ravassard et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2006)
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: The VR system constrains head movements to rotations in the horizontal plane.
source: Here, we present a VR system for mice in which a chronically implanted head-plate enables use of a holder that constrains head movements to rotations in the horizontal plane while the animal runs on a Styrofoam ball.
evidence: This is a description of the system design shown in Figure 1.

claim: Screens and projectors project a virtual environment in all horizontal directions around the mouse and onto the floor below it.
source: Screens and projectors project a virtual environment in all horizontal directions around the mouse, and onto the floor below it, from a viewpoint that moves with the rotation of the ball, following Aronov and Tank (2014) and Hölscher et al. (2005) (see Figure 1 and Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the VR display system shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mice displayed an initially lower running speed when first experiencing the real-world recording environment.
source: The mice displayed an initially lower running speed when first experiencing the real-world recording environment (a 60 × 60 cm square), but reached a higher average speed after 20 or so training trials.
evidence: This behavioral observation is supported by data in Figure 1F-H.

claim: The increase in running speed with experience was similar in virtual environments.
source: The increase in running speed with experience was similar in the virtual environments (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 1F-H.

claim: Running speeds did not differ between the 60 cm and 90 cm virtual environments.
source: Running speeds did not differ between the 60 cm and 90 cm virtual environments used for recording in seven and four of the mice, respectively (12.01 ± 2.77 in 60 cm VR, 14.33 ± 4.19 cm/s in 90 cm VR, p=0.29).
evidence: This comparison is stated with statistical test results.

claim: Running directions in VR showed a marginally greater unimodal bias compared to R.
source: Running directions in the VR environment showed a marginally greater unimodal bias compared to the real environment (R; Figure 1K).
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 1K.

claim: Mice displayed a greater tendency to run parallel to the four walls in VR.
source: Mice displayed a greater tendency to run parallel to the four walls in VR, a tendency which reduced with experience (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This behavioral observation is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mice took straighter, less tortuous paths in VR than in R.
source: They also took straighter, less tortuous, paths in VR than in R, as would be expected from their head-fixation (Figure 1L–N).
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 1L-N.

claim: Mice learned to approach the fixed reward location in the fading beacon task.
source: They learned to approach the fixed reward location and could do so even after it became completely unmarked (fully faded, see Figure 2 and Video 1 of a mouse performing the task, and Materials and methods for details of the training regime).
evidence: This learning is demonstrated in Figure 2 and Video 1.

claim: 231 CA1 cells were recorded from seven mice.
source: We recorded a total of 231 CA1 cells from seven mice
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of cells recorded.

claim: 179 cells were classified as place cells in the real environment.
source: 179 cells were classified as place cells in the real environment
evidence: This is a direct statement of cell classification.

claim: 185 cells were classified as place cells in the virtual environment.
source: 185 cells in the virtual environment
evidence: This is a direct statement of cell classification.

claim: 154 cells were classified as place cells in both real and virtual environments.
source: and 154 cells were classified as place cells in both real and virtual environments
evidence: This is a direct statement of cell classification.

claim: 141 cells were recorded in dorsomedial Entorhinal Cortex from eight mice.
source: We recorded 141 cells in dorsomedial Entorhinal Cortex (dmEC) from eight mice
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of cells recorded.

claim: 82 cells were classified as grid cells in the real environment.
source: 82 of them were classified as grid cells in the real environment
evidence: This is a direct statement of cell classification.

claim: 65 cells were classified as grid cells in the virtual environment.
source: 65 of them grid cells in the virtual environment
evidence: This is a direct statement of cell classification.

claim: 61 cells were classified as grid cells in both real and virtual environments.
source: and 61 were classified as grid cells in both real and virtual environments
evidence: This is a direct statement of cell classification.

claim: 16 cells were quantified as head-direction cells in R.
source: Among these 141 recorded cells, 16 cells were quantified as head-direction cells (HDCs) in R
evidence: This is a direct statement of cell classification.

claim: 20 cells were quantified as head-direction cells in VR.
source: 20 cells were HDCs in VR
evidence: This is a direct statement of cell classification.

claim: 12 cells were classified as head-direction cells in both R and VR.
source: with 12 cells classified as HDCs in both real ('R') and virtual reality ('VR') environments
evidence: This is a direct statement of cell classification.

claim: Place cells recorded from CA1 showed spatially localized firing in the virtual environment.
source: Place cells recorded from CA1 showed spatially localized firing in the virtual environment, with similar firing rates in the virtual and real square environments.
evidence: This is stated and demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: Place cells had similar firing rates in VR and R.
source: Place cells recorded from CA1 showed spatially localized firing in the virtual environment, with similar firing rates in the virtual and real square environments.
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Place cells had larger firing fields in VR than in R by a factor of 1.44.
source: Place cells had larger firing fields in VR than in R, by a factor 1.44 (field size in VR/field size in R).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The spatial information content of place cell firing fields in VR was lower than in R.
source: The spatial information content of firing fields in VR was lower than in R.
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The firing of place cells was more strongly directionally modulated in VR than in R.
source: In addition, the firing of place cells was more strongly directionally modulated in VR than in R (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Similar place cell results were seen irrespective of whether recordings took place in 60×60 cm or 90×90 cm VR environments.
source: Similar results were seen irrespective of whether recordings took place in the 60 × 60 cm or 90 × 90 cm VR environments (e.g. the place field expansion factor being 1.44 in 90 cm, 1.43 in 60 cm, p=0.66, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This comparison is stated with statistical results and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Apparent directionality in place cell firing can arise from inhomogeneous sampling of direction within the firing field.
source: One possible contribution to apparent directionality in place cell firing could be inhomogeneous sampling of direction within the (locational) firing field.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological consideration supported by citation to Burgess et al., 2005.

claim: Using the pxd model procedure did not ameliorate the directionality in place cell firing.
source: However, using this procedure did not ameliorate the directionality in firing (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3E (open bars).

claim: Firing directionality increased near boundaries in both VR and R.
source: Further analyses showed that firing directionality increased near to the boundaries in both virtual and real environments (where sampling of direction is particularly inhomogeneous)
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The additional directionality in VR compared to R was apparent also away from the boundaries.
source: but that the additional directionality in VR compared to R was apparent also away from the boundaries (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increased directionality of place cells in VR was present in both cylinder and square environments.
source: The increased directionality of place cells but not grid cells in VR was present in both cylinder and square environments, supporting the generality of the result (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Grid cells recorded in dmEC showed similar grid-like firing patterns in VR as in R.
source: Grid cells recorded in dmEC, showed similar grid-like firing patterns in VR as in R, with similar firing rates and 'gridness' scores.
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Grid cells had similar firing rates in VR and R.
source: Grid cells recorded in dmEC, showed similar grid-like firing patterns in VR as in R, with similar firing rates and 'gridness' scores.
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Grid cells had similar gridness scores in VR and R.
source: Grid cells recorded in dmEC, showed similar grid-like firing patterns in VR as in R, with similar firing rates and 'gridness' scores.
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The spatial scale of grids was larger in VR than in R with an average increase of 1.42.
source: The spatial scale of the grids was larger in VR than in R, with an average increase of 1.42 (grid scale in VR/grid scale in R, n = 6 mice).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The spatial information content of grid cell firing was lower in VR than R.
source: The spatial information content of grid cell firing was lower in VR than R, as with the place cells.
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Grid cells showed a slight decrease in directionality from R to VR.
source: Unlike the place cells, the grid cells showed a slight decrease in directionality from R to VR
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4G (solid bars).

claim: The decrease in grid cell directionality was not seen when controlling for inhomogeneous sampling in a pxd model.
source: although this appears to reflect inhomogeneous sampling of directions within firing fields, as the effect was not seen when controlling for this in a joint 'pxd' model (see Figure 4)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4G (open bars).

claim: Similar grid cell results were seen irrespective of whether recordings took place in 60×60 cm or 90×90 cm VR environments.
source: Similar results were seen irrespective of whether recordings took place in the 60 × 60 cm or 90 × 90 cm VR environments (e.g. the grid scale expansion factor being 1.43 in 60 cm, 1.36 in 90 cm, p=0.78)
evidence: This comparison is stated with statistical results.

claim: There was no difference in directional information in individual grid firing fields between R and VR.
source: Accordingly, we checked the directional information in the firing of each field, without finding any difference between R and VR (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The differences in firing properties between R and VR are similar when R trials both preceded and followed VR trials.
source: Under these conditions, the differences in firing properties between R and VR are similar to those shown in Figures 3 and 4, again indicating generality.
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Grid cells in the second group showed lower gridness scores in VR than R.
source: However, the 20 grid cells in this group did show lower gridness scores in VR than R
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the additional experiment.

claim: 43 cells were classified as grid cells in R but only 24 as grid cells in VR in the second group.
source: and 43 cells were classified as grid cells in R but only 24 as grid cells in VR
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the additional experiment.

claim: Grid cell firing patterns can be sensitive to the use of VR and the inherent conflict between virtual and uncontrolled cues to translation.
source: Thus, grid cell firing patterns can be sensitive to the use of VR and the inherent conflict between virtual and uncontrolled cues to translation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed differences in grid cell properties.

claim: The extra sensitivity in the second group of animals might reflect their greater age at test.
source: The extra sensitivity in the second group of animals might reflect their greater age at test (mice with grid cells, main experiment: n = 8, age = 25.4 ± 4.3 weeks; additional experiment: n = 3, age = 40.1 ± 11.2 weeks; t(9)=-3.34, p<0.01) but this would require further verification.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with statistical comparison.

claim: Head-direction cells were recorded in dmEC.
source: We also recorded head-direction cells in the dmEC, as previously reported in rats (Sargolini et al., 2006) and mice (Fyhn et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Head-direction cells showed similar firing rates in VR and R.
source: These cells showed similar firing rates in VR and R, with similar tuning widths (see Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Head-direction cells showed similar tuning widths in VR and R.
source: These cells showed similar firing rates in VR and R, with similar tuning widths (see Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The relative differences in tuning directions of simultaneously recorded directional cells was maintained between R and VR.
source: The relative differences in the tuning directions of simultaneously recorded directional cells was maintained between R and VR, even though the absolute tuning direction was not (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absolute tuning direction of head-direction cells was not maintained between R and VR.
source: The relative differences in the tuning directions of simultaneously recorded directional cells was maintained between R and VR, even though the absolute tuning direction was not (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Translational movement defining location within the virtual environment purely reflects feedback from the virtual reality system.
source: The translational movement defining location within the virtual environment purely reflects feedback (visual, motoric and proprioceptive) from the virtual reality system, as location within the real world does not change.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the VR system.

claim: The animal's sense of orientation might reflect both virtual and real-world inputs.
source: However, the animal's sense of orientation might reflect both virtual and real-world inputs, as the animal rotates in both the real and virtual world.
evidence: This is a logical inference about orientation cues.

claim: A 180° rotation of the virtual environment and entry point resulted in corresponding rotation of virtual firing patterns of place, grid and head-direction cells.
source: In separate trials, we observed a corresponding rotation of the virtual firing patterns of place, grid and head-direction cells, indicating the primacy of the virtual environment over non-controlled real world cues (see Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated and demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: All grid and head direction cells followed the rotation of VR cues.
source: While all the grid and head direction cells followed the rotation of VR cues (and entry point), a small percentage of place cells (7/141; 5%) did not.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the rotation experiment.

claim: A small percentage of place cells (7/141; 5%) did not follow the rotation of VR cues.
source: While all the grid and head direction cells followed the rotation of VR cues (and entry point), a small percentage of place cells (7/141; 5%) did not.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the rotation experiment.

claim: Place cells that did not rotate show much lower spatial information scores in both R and VR conditions.
source: These place cells show much lower spatial information scores in both the R and VR conditions (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lack of rotation in some place cells might result from their weaker or less stable spatial tuning to proximal environmental cues.
source: indicating that their lack of rotation might be the result of their weaker or less stable spatial tuning to the proximal environmental cues that were rotated.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lower spatial information scores.

claim: Running speed correlates with firing rates of place cells, grid cells and speed cells.
source: The animal's running speed is known to correlate with the firing rates of cells, including place cells, grid cells and (by definition) speed cells (Sargolini et al., 2006; McNaughton et al., 1983; Kropff et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Running speed correlates with the frequency of the local field potential theta rhythm.
source: and with the frequency of the local field potential theta rhythm (McFarland et al., 1975; Rivas et al., 1996; Sławińska and Kasicki, 1998)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The slope of the relationship between theta frequency and running speed was reduced within VR compared to R.
source: We found that the slope of the relationship between theta frequency and running speed was reduced within the VR compared to R
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: The slope of the relationship between firing rates and running speed was not reduced in VR for place, grid and speed cells.
source: while this was not the case for the firing rates of place, grid and speed cells (see Figure 7)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 7C-F.

claim: Changes in grid scale and theta frequency in VR versus R did not correlate significantly across animals.
source: However, the changes in grid scale and theta frequency in virtual versus real environments did not correlate with each other significantly across animals.
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from correlation analysis.

claim: There was an effect of running speed on the sizes of place and grid fields that was similar in R and VR.
source: There was an effect of running speed on the sizes of place and grid fields that was similar in R and VR
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of running speed on field size was not the monotonic relationship predicted by an effect of theta frequency on field size.
source: but was not the monotonic relationship that would be predicted by an effect of (speed-related) theta frequency on field size (see Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Theta phase precession is an important aspect of place and grid cell firing.
source: Finally, an important aspect of place and grid cell firing is the temporal coding seen in the theta phase precession of firing in 1-d (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Hafting et al., 2008) and 2-d (Climer et al., 2015; Jeewajee et al., 2014) environments.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Theta modulated firing frequency is slightly higher than LFP frequency in both R and VR, consistent with theta phase precession.
source: This analysis shows that, despite the lower overall frequencies in VR, theta modulated firing frequency is slightly higher than the LFP frequency in both R and VR, consistent with theta phase precession (see Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Normal 2-d phase precession was found in place and grid cells with clear theta-modulation in both VR and R.
source: In addition, we directly analysed phase precession in place and grid cells with clear theta-modulation, finding normal 2-d phase precession in both VR and in R (as in 1-d VR [Harvey et al., 2009]).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 8B-E, with citation to previous work.

claim: The phase precession slope is lower in VR, consistent with larger firing fields overall in VR environments.
source: The phase precession slope is lower in VR, consistent with larger firing fields overall in VR environments
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 8D-E.

claim: Correlations between phase precession slope and field size only reached significance for place cells in R.
source: but correlations between slope and field size only reached significance for place cells in R (n = 38, r = 0.46, p<0.01; all other p>0.3, see Figure 8B–E)
evidence: This is stated with statistical results.

claim: Theta phase precession in place and grid cells is independent of linear vestibular acceleration signals.
source: These results indicate that theta phase precession in place and grid cells is independent of linear vestibular acceleration signals and the absolute value of theta frequency.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the presence of phase precession in VR despite absent vestibular cues.

claim: Theta phase precession in place and grid cells is independent of the absolute value of theta frequency.
source: These results indicate that theta phase precession in place and grid cells is independent of linear vestibular acceleration signals and the absolute value of theta frequency.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the presence of phase precession in VR despite reduced theta frequency.

claim: The VR system allows expression of spatial learning and memory in open environments.
source: We have demonstrated the ability of a novel mouse virtual reality (VR) system to allow expression of spatial learning and memory in open environments, following related work in rats (Aronov and Tank, 2014; Hölscher et al., 2005; Cushman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the behavioral data and citations to related work.

claim: In the fading-beacon task, mice learned to return to a rewarded spatial location from multiple novel starting locations.
source: Specifically, in the fading-beacon task, mice learned to return to a rewarded spatial location from multiple novel starting locations which (once the beacon had faded) was not marked by any proximal sensory stimulus, that is requiring allocentric spatial memory.
evidence: This is stated and demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: The fading-beacon task requires allocentric spatial memory.
source: which (once the beacon had faded) was not marked by any proximal sensory stimulus, that is requiring allocentric spatial memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the task requirements.

claim: The VR system allows expression of characteristic spatially modulated firing patterns of place, grid and head-direction cells in open arenas.
source: Importantly, we also demonstrated that the VR system allows expression of the characteristic spatially modulated firing patterns of place, grid and head-direction cells in open arenas.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the electrophysiological data in Figures 3-5.

claim: The VR system passes the first pre-requisite as a tool for studying mechanisms behind two dimensional firing patterns of spatial cells.
source: Thus, it passes the first pre-requisite as a tool for studying the mechanisms behind the two dimensional firing patterns of these spatial cells, following previous systems for rats that also allow physical rotation of the animal (Aronov and Tank, 2014; Hölscher et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated spatial firing patterns, with citations to related systems.

claim: The LFP theta frequency reflects a contribution from vestibular translational acceleration signals.
source: The LFP theta frequency reflects a contribution from vestibular translational acceleration signals (Ravassard et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2006) which will be absent in our VR system.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Vestibular translational acceleration signals are absent in the VR system.
source: The LFP theta frequency reflects a contribution from vestibular translational acceleration signals (Ravassard et al., 2013; Russell et al., 2006) which will be absent in our VR system.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the VR system.

claim: There was no change in the increasing firing rates of place, grid and speed cells with running speed in VR.
source: However, there was no change in the increasing firing rates of place, grid and speed cells with running speed in VR (Figure 7), indicating an independence from vestibular translational acceleration cues.
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 7C-F.

claim: The firing rate modulation with speed indicates independence from vestibular translational acceleration cues.
source: However, there was no change in the increasing firing rates of place, grid and speed cells with running speed in VR (Figure 7), indicating an independence from vestibular translational acceleration cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the similarity of firing rate modulation in VR and R.

claim: The absence of linear acceleration signals may affect both LFP theta rhythmicity and spatial scale of firing patterns.
source: Thus, it is possible that the absence of linear acceleration signals affects both LFP theta rhythmicity and the spatial scale of firing patterns, but there was no evidence that the two were directly related.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed changes.

claim: There was no evidence that theta frequency and spatial scale changes were directly related.
source: Thus, it is possible that the absence of linear acceleration signals affects both LFP theta rhythmicity and the spatial scale of firing patterns, but there was no evidence that the two were directly related.
evidence: This is stated based on the lack of correlation between the two measures.

claim: Uncontrolled distal cues will conflict with virtual cues indicating self-motion.
source: Finally, uncontrolled distal cues, such as sounds and smells, and the visual appearance of the apparatus aside from the screens (the edge of the ball, the edges of the screens) will conflict with virtual cues indicating self-motion.
evidence: This is a statement about potential confounding factors in the VR system.

claim: Increased firing field size could reflect broader tuning or reduced precision due to absent or conflicting inputs.
source: Thus, increased firing field size could also reflect broader tuning or reduced precision due to absent or conflicting inputs, consistent with the reduced spatial information seen in place and grid cell firing patterns (Figures 3 and 4)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to Towse et al., 2014.

claim: More grid cells met the spatial firing criteria in R than in VR.
source: Nonetheless, more grid cells met the spatial firing criteria in R than in VR, which was not true for place or head-direction cells
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the classification results.

claim: Lower gridness scores in VR would be consistent with conflict in translational cues if grid cell firing specifically reflects translational self-motion.
source: This would be consistent with the presence of conflict in translational cues in VR (e.g. vestibular versus optic flow) if grid cell firing specifically reflects translational self-motion (McNaughton et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Head direction cells do not show broader tuning in VR probably because there is no absence of vestibular rotation cues and no conflict with distal real-world cues.
source: The head direction cells do not show broader tuning in the VR (Figure 5), probably because there is no absence of vestibular rotation cues and no conflict with distal real-world cues, as the mice rotate similarly in the virtual and real world.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the nature of rotational cues in the VR system.

claim: Spatial firing patterns follow the virtual cues when virtual cues and entry point are put into conflict with uncontrolled real-world cues.

claim: Reliable within-trial local cues may contribute to localization of firing in real-world experiments.
source: Experimenters typically work hard to remove consistent uncontrolled cues from real-world experiments (e.g. cleaning and rotating the walls and floor between trials), but reliable within-trial local cues (e.g. olfactory, tactile) may contribute to localization of firing nonetheless (Ravassard et al., 2013).

claim: Uncontrolled local cues in real experiments may support orientation-independent locational response that can be bound to distinct visual scenes observed in different directions.
source: Thus uncontrolled local cues in real experiments may be useful for supporting an orientation-independent locational response that can be bound to the distinct visual scenes observed in different directions, see also Acharya et al., (2016).

claim: By removing local cues, VR leaves locational responses of place cells more prone to modulation by directionally specific visual cues.
source: In this case, by removing these local cues, the use of VR leaves the locational responses of place cells more prone to modulation by the remaining (directionally specific) visual cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why place cells show increased directionality in VR.

However, this would need to be verified in future work.

claim: VR enables manipulations that are impossible in the real-world.
source: In conclusion, by using VR, the system presented here offers advantages over traditional paradigms by enabling manipulations that are impossible in the real-world, allowing visual projection of an environment that need not directly reflect a physical reality or the animals' movements.
